card.m: Measure the grain sizes in sand

panelTexts.text: A sieve analysis measures how big the grains in a sample are. Labs report it as the particle size distribution, or PSD. Sand plants, concrete labs and foundries rely on this test to check their materials.

A pile of sand isn’t the same all the way through: big grains and fine grains separate. Pour it through the riffle splitter, which divides it into two matching halves, keep one half, and split again until you have about 100 grams.
Done. Two splits took the pile down to one representative portion of about 100 grams.

Dry the sample in the oven at about 110 °C until its mass stops changing, and let it cool. Then press TARE with the empty dish on the balance, so the reading only counts the sand, and pour the sample in.

Nest the sieves with the biggest openings on top and the finest at the bottom, with a pan underneath to catch the dust. Sieves are named by their US mesh number, roughly the number of openings per inch.

Pour the sample onto the top sieve, put the cover on, clamp the stack and press START. The shaker swirls and taps the stack so every grain gets its chance to fall through. Labs often shake for 10 to 15 minutes; this run is sped up.
Shaking finished. The grains have settled onto the sieves that were too fine for them to pass.
Lift the sieves off one at a time, from the top, and weigh what stayed on each. The balance is tared for each empty sieve, so it reads the retained mass.
Teal line: % passing each sieve. Gold bars: % retained on each sieve.

The AFS grain fineness number sums each sieve’s % retained times a multiplier, then divides by the total. A bigger number means finer sand. Plants compare it, and the whole curve, against each customer’s spec.

card.m: Find the concentration of a mystery acid

panelTexts.text: A titration finds how concentrated a solution is by reacting it with another solution whose concentration you already know. Here, sodium hydroxide (a base) neutralizes a mystery hydrochloric acid.
Phenolphthalein, the indicator, stays colorless in acid and turns pink once the solution turns slightly basic, at about pH 8.2.
In a real lab: goggles on. Both chemicals can burn skin and eyes.

Pour exactly 25.00 mL of the mystery acid into the flask and add 2 drops of phenolphthalein. Fill the burette with 0.1000 M sodium hydroxide, then read the starting volume at the bottom of the curved liquid surface, the meniscus, with your eye level with it.

Hold the flask and swirl it as the base runs in. Add base fast at first. When pink flashes start to linger, slow down and finish one drop at a time. The endpoint is the first drop that keeps the whole flask faint pink for 30 seconds.
The pH jumps from about 4 to 10 within a drop or two of the equivalence point. That steep jump is why one indicator color change can pin down the answer so precisely.

toasts: Turn the stopcock to add base: a milliliter, a tenth, or one drop.
No lasting pink yet. Keep adding base.

card.m: Measure gravity with a string and a weight

panelTexts.text: A pendulum’s swing time depends on its length and on gravity, but not on how heavy the bob is. Time 10 full swings, and you can work out the strength of gravity, g.
The math: one swing takes T = 2π√(L ÷ g), so g = 4π²L ÷ T².
Set the length from the pivot to the center of the bob. Then take hold of the bob, pull it back to the release angle, keep it still and let go. The photogate counts 10 full swings (there and back).
Swinging… The photogate times each pass. Let it finish 10 full swings.
Your data
Try two more lengths, like 0.50 m and 1.50 m. Plotting T² against L gives a straight line, and its slope gives g.

card.m: Build a model car or building

panelTexts.text: Pick a kit. You’ll build it with your own hands, one part at a time, the way you would with real materials, then test it.
The Automobile and Building blueprints on the walls show the real versions of these parts.

card.m: Build a mini world, one layer at a time

panelTexts.text: You built a world, layer by layer. Every 3D game, film and XR app is made with these same layers.

card.m: Where every treatment begins and ends

panelTexts.text: A dialysis patient's bloodstream is opened at every treatment, so the single most effective protection against infection is clean hands. Every session begins and ends at this sink.
Wet your hands, soap them, and scrub for at least twenty seconds: palms, backs, between the fingers and under the nails. Rinse, dry with a paper towel, and use the towel to turn off the tap.
Gloves go on last and come off first. A gown and a face shield protect you wherever a line could spray. Change gloves between every patient and every task.
A technician keeps a clean field, the supplies and the machine's connections, and a dirty one, the used lines and the bins. Nothing crosses back from dirty to clean.

card.m: Prime it, fit the dialyzer, check the prescription

panelTexts.text: A pump moves the patient's blood through the dialyzer, where waste and extra water pass into the dialysate, and the cleaned blood returns. The machine watches pressures, temperature and conductivity the whole time.
Turn the machine on and let it run its own checks: the alarms, the pumps, the air detector. A machine that fails a check is not used that day.
Hang the saline, thread the blood lines through the pump and the air detector, and prime them until no bubbles remain. Air in the line is the alarm you never want to hear.
The cartridge is the artificial kidney: thousands of hollow fibres in a clear case. Fit it in its holder, connect the lines and check that it is the type the order asks for.
The patient's dialysate mix, flow rate, treatment time and fluid removal are set from the order. Every number is read twice, and the second reading is by a second person.

card.m: Weight, blood pressure, the access, and watching

panelTexts.text: A patient's weight before treatment tells you how much fluid to remove, so the scale is the first stop. Record it against their dry weight.
Take them seated and record them. A change from the patient's usual is reported before treatment starts, not after.
The fistula, graft or catheter is the patient's lifeline. Look at it, listen for the thrill and the bruit, and keep it clean. Only trained hands connect to it.
Through the treatment you check vitals every thirty minutes and watch for cramps, dizziness or bleeding. The patient is the best monitor there is: ask how they feel.

card.m: Carbon, softener, reverse osmosis, and the log

panelTexts.text: A patient meets hundreds of litres of dialysate a week, so the water it is made from has to be cleaner than drinking water. This panel is where that is checked.
The carbon tanks take out chlorine and chloramine, the softener takes out hardness, and reverse osmosis takes out nearly everything else. Each stage protects the next.
Each shift: the chlorine test after the carbon tanks, the conductivity and the pressure on the RO unit, and the temperature. A failed test stops treatment until it is fixed.
Every reading goes in the log with the time and your initials. The log is a legal record and the clinic's memory.

card.m: The flowsheet, written as you go

panelTexts.text: Every treatment has a record: the vitals, the machine settings, the alarms, and what was done about each one.
Numbers written at the time are right. Numbers written at the end of the shift are guesses. Chart each check when you make it.
At the end of the shift the next technician reads your notes before they meet the patient. Clear, complete, and signed.
